passages.title: The Return of the Night Sky
body: For almost all of human history, a clear night revealed thousands of stars and the pale band of the Milky Way. Today, more than a third of the world's population, and the large majority of people in Europe and North America, can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. The cause is not air pollution or cloud, but light: the glow of streetlights, buildings, advertising and car parks, scattered back down to the ground by particles in the atmosphere. Astronomers call this skyglow.

Skyglow was first treated as a serious problem by astronomers rather than by environmental scientists. As cities expanded in the twentieth century, observatories that had been built on the edges of towns found their telescopes almost useless. Several major observatories were moved to remote mountains, and some cities near them agreed to limit outdoor lighting. These early agreements were narrow in scope, aimed only at protecting scientific research, but they showed that lighting could be controlled without making streets unsafe.

Since the 1990s, research has widened the debate. Biologists have shown that artificial light at night disrupts the behaviour of a wide range of animals. Newly hatched sea turtles, which find the ocean by moving towards the brightest horizon, are drawn inland towards hotels and roads. Migrating birds circle lit buildings until they are exhausted. Many insects are attracted to lamps and die there, and because insects pollinate plants and feed other animals, the effects spread through entire ecosystems. Studies of humans have linked bright light late in the evening to disturbed sleep, although the long-term health effects remain debated.

Perhaps surprisingly, the most significant change in outdoor lighting in recent years has made the problem both better and worse. Cities around the world have replaced older sodium lamps with light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, which use far less electricity. Because LEDs can be aimed precisely, a well-designed fitting sends light only downwards, onto the road. However, many early LED installations produced a cold, bluish-white light, and blue light scatters in the atmosphere more strongly than the orange light of sodium lamps. In addition, because LEDs are cheap to run, some councils and businesses have simply installed more of them. Satellite measurements suggest that the area of the Earth's surface that is artificially lit at night has continued to grow by around two per cent a year.

The solutions are, in principle, simple and inexpensive. Lights can be shielded so that no light escapes above the horizontal. Warmer colours, with less blue, can be chosen. Lights can be dimmed late at night, when streets are nearly empty, or switched on only when sensors detect a person or vehicle. Some towns that have adopted these measures report reductions in energy costs of more than half, with no measurable increase in crime or road accidents.

A growing number of places have also chosen to market their darkness. Dark sky reserves, where lighting is strictly managed, now attract visitors who travel specifically to see the stars, and local hotels and guides have found that astronomy brings tourists in winter, a season that was previously quiet. Supporters argue that a starry sky should be considered part of a region's natural heritage, in the same way as a coastline or a forest. Whether that view spreads beyond a few enthusiastic communities will depend on persuading ordinary residents that a darker street can also be a safer and more pleasant one.

passages.title: The Salt Roads
body: A. Salt is so cheap and plentiful today that it is hard to imagine it was once among the most valuable goods in the world. Yet for thousands of years, salt shaped where people settled, which cities grew rich and which roads were built. The reason is biological as much as economic: humans and their animals need salt to survive, and before refrigeration, salt was the main way of preserving meat and fish through the winter.

B. Salt can be obtained in three main ways: by evaporating seawater in shallow pools, by boiling water from salty springs, or by mining rock salt from underground deposits left by ancient seas. Each method required heavy labour or large amounts of fuel, and the best sources were often far from the people who needed salt most. Inland farming communities, in particular, depended on supplies carried over long distances.

C. The routes along which salt travelled became some of the oldest trade roads in Europe, Africa and Asia. In the Sahara, camel caravans carried slabs of rock salt south from desert mines to the markets of West Africa, where it was exchanged for gold, sometimes, according to early travellers, at equal weight. Although modern historians believe such accounts were exaggerated, there is no doubt that salt and gold were the two pillars of a trade that made cities such as Timbuktu wealthy centres of learning.

D. Governments soon realised that a product everyone needed was an ideal thing to tax. In China, a state monopoly on salt was established more than two thousand years ago and provided a large share of imperial revenue for centuries. In France, a hated salt tax known as the gabelle required every household to buy a minimum quantity of salt each year at a fixed price, regardless of need. Smuggling was widespread, and punishments for it were severe.

E. Salt also left its mark on language. Many place names in England that end in -wich, such as Northwich and Droitwich, were once centres of salt production. The word salary is often said to come from a Roman payment to soldiers for buying salt, although scholars point out that there is little direct evidence for this popular story.

F. The importance of salt began to decline in the nineteenth century, for two reasons. First, geologists discovered enormous underground deposits in many countries, and new drilling techniques allowed salt to be extracted cheaply by pumping water into the deposits and bringing up brine. Second, canning and, later, refrigeration reduced the need to preserve food with large quantities of salt. Within a few decades, a precious commodity became an everyday one.

G. Today, less than a fifth of the salt produced worldwide is eaten. The majority is used by the chemical industry, to make products such as plastics and glass, and a large amount is spread on roads in cold countries to melt ice. The old salt roads survive mainly as walking routes and in local museums, reminders of a time when a handful of white crystals could decide the fortunes of a city.

passages.title: Why We Forget
body: We tend to think of forgetting as a failure, a sign that memory has let us down. Students forget what they studied, adults forget names and appointments, and the fear of memory loss in old age is widespread. Yet a growing body of research suggests that forgetting is not simply the opposite of remembering. In many cases it appears to be an active and useful process, one that a healthy brain could not do without.

The scientific study of forgetting began in the 1880s with Hermann Ebbinghaus, who taught himself long lists of meaningless syllables and then tested how many he could recall after different intervals. He found that most forgetting happened quickly, within the first hour or so, after which the rate slowed considerably. His 'forgetting curve' has been reproduced many times since. It is worth remembering, however, that Ebbinghaus deliberately studied material with no meaning, and meaningful information is generally retained far better.

For much of the twentieth century, two explanations competed. According to decay theory, memories simply fade with time, like footprints in sand. According to interference theory, memories are lost because other memories get in the way: old knowledge makes new learning harder, and new learning disrupts old knowledge. The psychologist John Jenkins and his colleague Karl Dallenbach provided early support for interference in the 1920s, when they showed that people who slept after learning remembered more than those who stayed awake, presumably because sleep protected them from new, competing experiences.

More recent work has shifted the emphasis again. The neuroscientist Oliver Hardt and his colleagues have argued that the brain contains mechanisms whose purpose is to remove memories. If every experience were stored permanently and in equal detail, they suggest, retrieving useful information would become slow and confused. Forgetting the details of an ordinary journey to work, for example, allows us to remember the general route without being distracted by every individual trip.

Experiments on decision-making point in the same direction. The neuroscientist Blake Richards, working with Paul Frankland, has drawn on computer models to argue that a memory system which forgets some information can make better predictions in a changing environment than one which remembers everything. A system that holds on too tightly to the past, the models suggest, struggles to adapt when circumstances change. Forgetting, in this view, is the price of flexibility, and a price worth paying.

None of this means that all forgetting is good. Diseases such as dementia destroy memories that people need and value, and the distress they cause is very real. But the research does suggest that our attitude to everyday forgetting may be too harsh. Practical advice for learners follows from it. Because forgetting is fastest soon after learning, reviewing new material within a day, and then at gradually increasing intervals, is far more effective than reading it many times in a single session. Each review, made at the moment when the memory is starting to fade, appears to strengthen it more than an easy review would. In other words, a little forgetting may be exactly what makes long-term learning possible.
